title: Distributed Audio and AV with Sonos and Control4
content:
## Two Architectures
Distributed audio comes in two flavors:
- **Networked/streaming (Sonos)**: each zone has a self-contained streaming amp; control is app-based over the LAN/Wi-Fi.
- **Centralized matrix (Control4)**: amplifiers and sources live in the rack; audio is distributed over structured wiring to keypads, touchscreens, and in-ceiling speakers.

### Sonos Approach
- Use a **Sonos Amp** (125W/ch, drives in-ceiling/in-wall passive speakers) per zone, or **Sonos Architectural** by Sonance speakers.
- **Wire the Amp via Ethernet** (not just Wi-Fi) into the `UniFi` switch — SonosNet/streaming is far more reliable hardwired, and PoE-adjacent zones benefit from clean network paths.
- Speaker wire: **16 AWG** for runs under ~50 ft, **14 AWG** for longer/4-ohm loads. Observe polarity (+/-) at every connection.
- Group zones in the Sonos app; integrate with `UniFi` VLANs (keep AV on a stable subnet with mDNS/Bonjour reflection enabled across VLANs).

### Control4 Approach
- Central **Control4 Director** controller (e.g., `Control4 CA-1` or EA series) + a **multi-zone amplifier** in the rack.
- Home-run **16/14 AWG speaker wire** from each ceiling speaker pair to the rack matrix amp.
- **Cat6** to each keypad/touchscreen for control + IP.
- Programmed with **Composer Pro**: bind sources, zones, and scenes; integrate lighting (`Lutron RadioRA 2`), shades, and HVAC into unified scenes.

## Speaker Layout
- In-ceiling speakers spaced so coverage circles overlap — typically **8-10 ft** on center for even fill; pull them ~**2-3 ft** off walls.
- Match **impedance**: most amps want **8 ohm**; parallel pairs can drop to 4 ohm — verify the amp tolerates it.
- For 70V distributed (large commercial), use a **70V transformer-tapped** speaker system instead of low-impedance home runs.

## Cabling and Rack
- Use **CL2/CL3-rated** in-wall speaker cable (NEC 725).
- Label both ends of every speaker and control run.
- Provide rack ventilation and a **UPS** for controllers/amps.
- Keep speaker runs away from parallel power; star-ground the rack.

## Commissioning
- Set zone levels and EQ; verify polarity with a polarity tester (out-of-phase pairs cancel bass).
- Test each source-to-zone path and every control surface/scene.
- For Sonos, run **Trueplay** room tuning where supported.
- Document zones, speaker tap settings, and source mapping in the CRM and train the client on the app/keypads.

## Best Practices
- Hardwire everything you can — Wi-Fi-only multiroom audio is the top callback source.
- Standardize on one control ecosystem per project to avoid integration gaps.

title: Troubleshooting PoE and Network Connectivity Faults
content:
## Work the OSI Layers Bottom-Up
Most field network faults are **physical (Layer 1)**. Start there before blaming config.

### Layer 1 — Cabling and PoE
- **No link light**: check the patch cord first, then certify the run. A `Fluke Networks LinkIQ` or `MicroScanner` shows wiremap, length, and PoE class delivered.
- **Link but errors/CRC**: indicates a marginal termination or kinked cable. Re-terminate to T568B; verify twist maintained to the punchdown.
- **Exceeds 100 m**: links may negotiate but drop under load. Confirm the **90 m permanent link** limit (TIA-568).
- **Split pairs**: passes a basic continuity toner but fails certification (NEXT failure). Only a certifier or LinkIQ catches it.

### PoE-Specific Faults
- **Device won't power**: verify the switch port supports the needed class — **802.3af (15.4W)**, **at/PoE+ (30W)**, **bt/PoE++ (60-90W)**. A `UniFi U7` AP or PTZ camera may need PoE+ or ++.
- **Switch PoE budget exhausted**: a `UniFi Switch Pro 24 PoE` (~400W) can run out when fully loaded with high-draw APs/cameras. Check the **PoE Utilization** in the UniFi console; offload to a second switch.
- **Voltage drop on long runs**: PoE over a 90 m run loses voltage; a device near 100 m may boot-loop. Use Cat6A and/or a midspan injector.
- **Polarity/mode**: passive PoE injectors (non-802.3) can **damage** 802.3 gear — never mix. Confirm the injector matches the device standard.

### Layer 2/3 — Switching and IP
- **No IP / wrong VLAN**: confirm the port's VLAN/PVID in UniFi. A camera on the wrong VLAN won't reach the NVR.
- **Intermittent drops / broadcast storm**: a cabling loop. Enable **STP/RSTP** and check for a patch cord plugged port-to-port.
- **Duplicate IP**: two devices statically set the same address — check the DHCP lease table and reservations.
- **Slow throughput**: a port negotiated **100M instead of 1G** usually means a damaged pair (1G needs all 4 pairs; 100M needs only 2). Re-certify.

## A Repeatable Method
1. **Reproduce** and note which devices/ports are affected.
2. **Swap** the patch cord (free, fast win).
3. **Certify** the permanent link with `Fluke Networks`.
4. **Check the switch port**: speed, errors, PoE class, VLAN, in the `UniFi` console.
5. **Isolate** by moving the device to a known-good port.
6. **Document** the root cause in the CRM.

## Best Practices
- Keep a known-good test patch cord and a certifier on the truck.
- Watch interface error counters over time — rising CRCs predict failures.
- Never assume 'the cable is fine because it links' — Gigabit and PoE expose marginal runs that 100M tolerated.

title: Roughing In DWV: Slope, Pipe Sizing, and Vent Layout for a Full Bath
content:
## Drain-Waste-Vent Rough-In for a Standard Full Bath

A proper DWV rough-in is the backbone of any reliable plumbing system. Get the slope and venting wrong and you will chase slow drains, sewer gas, and siphoned traps for the life of the building.

### Pipe Sizing & Material

- **Toilet (water closet):** `3"` PVC DWV minimum. Use **Charlotte Pipe** Schedule 40 solid-core PVC. Never reduce below 3" on a WC drain.
- **Lavatory:** `1-1/2"` drain, `1-1/4"` trap arm minimum (1-1/2" preferred).
- **Tub/shower:** `2"` drain. A 2" trap on the shower prevents the slow-drain complaints common with 1-1/2".
- **Branch/main:** `3"` or `4"` to the stack depending on fixture-unit load.

### Slope (Grade)

The golden rule: **1/4" per foot** of fall on pipes 2-1/2" and smaller. For 3" through 6", `1/8" per foot` is acceptable and often preferred — too much slope on large pipe lets water outrun solids and causes clogs. Check fall with a 4-foot torpedo level (1" of fall over 4 ft = 1/4" per foot).

### Trap-Arm Length & Venting

Every trap needs a vent within the maximum developed length from the weir:

- `1-1/4"` trap arm: 5 ft max to vent
- `1-1/2"` trap arm: 6 ft max
- `2"` trap arm: 8 ft max
- `3"` trap arm: 12 ft max

Exceed these and the trap self-siphons, pulling the seal and letting sewer gas in.

### Step-by-Step

1. **Locate the closet flange** — 12" from finished wall to flange center for a standard rough-in. Set flange on top of finished floor.
2. **Run the 3" WC drain** to the stack, maintaining 1/4" per foot. Use long-sweep 1/4 bends and combo wyes — never a sanitary tee on its back for horizontal-to-horizontal.
3. **Tie lav and tub** into the branch with proper wye + 1/8 bend fittings.
4. **Stack the vent** — minimum `1-1/2"` individual vents, combining to a `2"` or `3"` vent through the roof. Vent terminal must be 6" above roof and 10 ft from / 3 ft above any window.
5. **Solvent-weld** all joints: purple primer, then PVC cement, quarter-turn the fitting.

### Pro Tips

- Dry-fit the entire assembly before cementing — DWV cement grabs in seconds.
- Support horizontal PVC every 4 ft with **Sioux Chief** clamps; support stacks at each floor.
- Keep a wet vent in mind for tight remodels: a 2" wet vent can serve the lav and vent the WC where code permits.

title: Water Supply Sizing and PEX vs. Copper: Choosing and Installing Distribution
content:
## Sizing and Installing Potable Water Distribution

Correct supply sizing keeps fixtures running at usable pressure under simultaneous demand. Under-size the main and the shower goes cold when someone flushes.

### Sizing by Fixture Units (WSFU)

Use the Hunter curve / IPC fixture-unit method:

- **3/4"** main typically serves a small home (up to ~20 WSFU at 40-60 PSI).
- **1"** main for larger homes or long runs.
- **1/2"** branches to most individual fixtures (lav, WC, shower).
- **3/4"** to tubs, hose bibs, and water heaters.

Keep velocity under **8 ft/s** (5 ft/s on hot lines) to prevent erosion and water hammer.

### PEX vs. Copper

**PEX-A (Uponor)** uses expansion fittings (ProPEX) — the tubing and ring expand, then shrink-fit onto the barb. Best freeze resistance and fewest flow restrictions.

**PEX-B (SharkBite, Apollo)** uses crimp (copper ring) or push-fit. Lower cost, slightly smaller ID at fittings.

**Type L copper** remains the premium for exposed/mechanical rooms and high-temp runs. Type M (thinner wall) is fine for most residential interior supply where allowed.

| Factor | PEX-A | Type L Copper |
|---|---|---|
| Freeze tolerance | Excellent | Poor (bursts) |
| Cost | Low | High |
| Connections | ProPEX expansion | Solder / ProPress |

### Manifold (Home-Run) vs. Trunk-and-Branch

A **home-run manifold** (Uponor or Sioux Chief) feeds each fixture with a dedicated 1/2" PEX line from a central manifold — balanced pressure, individual shutoffs, fast hot water. Trunk-and-branch uses fewer feet of pipe but shares pressure.

### Install Steps (Uponor PEX-A ProPEX)

1. Cut tubing square with a PEX cutter.
2. Slide the **ProPEX ring** flush to the tube end.
3. Expand with the Milwaukee M12 ProPEX expander — rotate between expansions.
4. Insert the fitting fully and hold 5-10 seconds while it shrinks back.
5. Pressure-test the system at **100 PSI** (or 1.5x working pressure) for a minimum of 15 minutes before close-in.

### Pro Tips

- Install **NIBCO** quarter-turn ball valves at the main and water heater.
- Add a **Watts** PRV if street pressure exceeds 80 PSI — code maximum at fixtures.
- Keep PEX 12" away from recessed-can heat and never expose it to UV.
- Use copper or brass stub-outs at fixtures for clean, durable connections.

title: Soldering, ProPress, and PEX Crimp: Three Joining Methods Done Right
content:
## Mastering the Three Core Copper/PEX Joining Methods

Every plumber needs all three. Choosing the right one per situation — and executing cleanly — separates leak-free work from callbacks.

### 1. Sweat Soldering (Type L/M Copper)

1. **Cut** square with a Ridgid tubing cutter; ream the burr.
2. **Clean** the pipe end and fitting socket to bright copper with emery cloth/fitting brush.
3. **Flux** both surfaces with a thin, even coat of water-soluble flux.
4. **Assemble** and heat with a MAPP/propane torch — heat the *fitting*, not the solder.
5. **Apply lead-free solder** (95/5 or Sn/Ag) when the pipe melts it — capillary action pulls it in. A 1/2" joint needs about 1/2" of solder.
6. **Wipe** and let cool undisturbed.

Key: drain the line. You cannot solder a joint with water in it — use a soldering bead or bread plug.

### 2. ProPress (Viega / NIBCO)

No flame — ideal in occupied/finished spaces.

1. Cut and ream.
2. **Mark insertion depth** on the pipe.
3. Confirm the fitting has its EPDM (water) or HNBR (gas) **O-ring** seated.
4. Insert pipe to the mark; the leak-before-press feature flags un-pressed joints.
5. Press with a **Ridgid RP 340/241** press tool and matching jaw until the tool cycles fully.

Faster than soldering and code-recognized; jaw size must match pipe size exactly.

### 3. PEX Crimp (SharkBite / Apollo PEX-B)

1. Cut PEX square.
2. Slide the **copper crimp ring** on, 1/8"-1/4" from the end.
3. Insert the barbed fitting fully.
4. Crimp perpendicular with the crimp tool until it bottoms out.
5. **Verify with the go/no-go gauge** — every joint, every time.

For PEX-A use Uponor ProPEX expansion instead (see distribution article).

### Common Mistakes

- **Overheating** solder joints burns the flux and causes pinholes — back off the flame as solder flows.
- Pressing over a **double O-ring** or debris in a ProPress fitting causes weeping; keep fittings clean.
- **Off-center crimps** on PEX fail the gauge — re-cut and redo, don't re-crimp.

### When to Use Which

- Mechanical room, exposed copper: **solder** (cheapest material).
- Finished/occupied, no flame allowed: **ProPress**.
- Concealed water distribution, speed: **PEX crimp/expansion**.

title: Tank and Tankless Water Heater Installation: Gas, Venting, and Condensate
content:
## Installing Storage and Tankless Water Heaters

Water heater installs combine plumbing, gas, venting, and (for high-efficiency units) condensate handling. Mistakes here cause CO hazards and floods.

### Storage Tank (Rheem / A.O. Smith / Bradford White)

- **Sizing:** 40-50 gal atmospheric for a 3-4 person home; check first-hour rating (FHR).
- **Cold/hot connections:** 3/4" with a **Watts** dielectric or brass nipples; install a NIBCO isolation valve on cold.
- **T&P valve:** Required. Run the discharge `3/4"` full-size, downward, terminating 6"-24" above the floor or to an approved drain — no traps, no threads on the end.
- **Expansion tank:** Required on closed systems (check valve/PRV present). Pre-charge to match supply PSI.
- **Drain pan:** Required where leakage damages structure; pipe to drain.

#### Atmospheric Venting

Draft hood units vent into a `3"`/4" Type B double-wall vent with proper rise and `1/4" per foot` upward slope to the chimney. Verify draft — backdrafting spills CO.

### Tankless (Rinnai / Navien / Noritz)

High-efficiency condensing units (e.g., **Navien NPE-240A2**, **Rinnai RU199**) are sealed-combustion.

- **Gas:** Condensing tankless needs **150,000-199,000 BTU/hr** — often a `3/4"` gas line is the minimum, but verify with a longest-run sizing table; many require an upsized meter/line.
- **Venting:** Category IV — use `2"` or `3"` PVC/CPVC or the manufacturer's polypropylene concentric. Maintain vent length limits (commonly up to 65-100 ft equivalent) and clearance from windows/intakes (min 12").
- **Condensate:** Condensing units produce acidic condensate (pH ~3). Route through a **neutralizer cartridge** to drain; never to bare metal.
- **Water:** 3/4" hot/cold with isolation/service valves (flush kit ports) for descaling.

### Commissioning

1. Fill tank fully and purge air before energizing — dry-firing destroys elements/burners.
2. Pressure/gas leak test joints with bubble solution.
3. Set temperature to **120°F** (anti-scald; reduces Legionella risk vs. lower).
4. Verify combustion/draft; on tankless, confirm error-free ignition and stable flame.

### Pro Tips

- Sediment-prone water: install a Sioux Chief drain pan and flush tanks annually.
- Add a **sediment trap (drip leg)** on the gas line ahead of the appliance.
- Strap tanks in seismic zones (two straps, upper/lower third).

title: Fixture Rough-In Dimensions: Toilets, Lavatories, Tubs, and Showers
content:
## Standard Fixture Rough-In Reference

Rough-in dimensions determine where supply and drain stub-outs land in the wall and floor. Set them wrong and the finished fixture won't fit or meet clearance code.

### Water Closet (Toilet)

- **Drain (flange):** Standard **12"** from finished wall to flange center. 10" and 14" rough-ins exist (verify the model — e.g., **TOTO Drake**, **Kohler Cimarron** are 12").
- **Supply stub:** 6" left of center, 6"-8" above finished floor.
- **Clearances (IPC/UPC):** Minimum **15"** from WC centerline to any side wall/fixture; **21"** clear in front (24" preferred).

### Lavatory (Bathroom Sink)

- **Drain stub:** Centered, ~`18"-19"` above finished floor (P-trap height).
- **Supply stubs:** 4" each side of drain center, ~`19"-21"` AFF.
- **Faucet:** Match holes to spread — 4" centerset or 8" widespread (e.g., **Delta**, **Moen**, **American Standard**).
- **Rim height:** 31"-36" typical.

### Tub / Shower

- **Tub drain:** At the head end, `2"` waste & overflow rough centered to the tub's drain location (typically 14"-16" from end wall).
- **Tub spout/valve:** Valve **28"** AFF (control), spout ~4" above tub rim, showerhead **78"** AFF for a standard install (raise for taller clients).
- **Shower drain:** 2" centered in the pan; pan slopes 1/4" per foot to drain.
- **Valve depth:** Set the **Moen Posi-Temp** or **Delta MultiChoice** rough-in valve to the plaster guard / finished-wall depth — too deep and the trim won't reach.

### Anti-Scald

Shower/tub valves must be **pressure-balancing or thermostatic** (ASSE 1016) limiting outlet to **120°F max**. Set the rotational limit stop during trim-out.

### Accessible (ADA) Notes

- Lav rim max **34"** AFF, knee clearance 27" min, insulate traps.
- WC centerline **16"-18"** from side wall; grab-bar blocking required.

### Pro Tips

- Always set the closet flange **on top** of finished floor, anchored to subfloor.
- Confirm the exact rough-in from the spec sheet of the actual fixture — **TOTO**, **Kohler**, and **American Standard** publish dimension drawings.
- Add backing/blocking for grab bars and wall-hung fixtures during rough-in, not after drywall.
materials_required: Moen Posi-Temp or Delta MultiChoice rough valve

title: Traps and Vents: Sizing, Trap Seals, and Prohibited Configurations
content:
## Trap and Vent Code Essentials

Traps hold a water seal that blocks sewer gas; vents protect that seal and let drains flow. Code is strict here because health and safety depend on it.

### Trap Requirements

- **One trap per fixture**, located as close as practical to the fixture outlet.
- **Trap seal depth:** `2" to 4"` of water (deeper allowed for evaporation-prone floor drains with trap primers).
- **Trap size = fixture drain size:** 1-1/4" lav, 1-1/2" tub/sink, 2" shower, 3" WC (integral trap).
- **Vertical distance** from fixture outlet to trap weir: **24" max** for a P-trap.

#### Prohibited Traps

- **S-traps** — self-siphon, banned.
- **Bell traps, drum traps, crown-vented traps** — prohibited.
- **Double trapping** a fixture — banned (creates an airlock).

### Vent Requirements

- **Trap-arm-to-vent max developed length** (the critical number):
  - 1-1/4" → 5 ft
  - 1-1/2" → 6 ft
  - 2" → 8 ft
  - 3" → 12 ft
- **Vent sizing:** Individual vent ≥ half the drain diameter, never less than `1-1/4"`.
- **Stack vent / vent through roof:** Size per total drainage fixture units; `2"` or `3"` typical for residential.

### Vent Types

- **Individual (revent):** One per fixture, simplest and most reliable.
- **Wet vent:** A drain that also vents an adjacent fixture — common bathroom-group method; the wet-vented section must be upsized (often 2").
- **Air admittance valve (AAV):** **Studor/Sioux Chief** one-way valve for islands/remodels where a conventional vent is impractical — allowed by IPC, restricted/banned by some UPC jurisdictions. Must be accessible and 4" above the trap arm.

### Vent Termination

- Min `6"` above roof (12" in snow regions).
- **10 ft** from / **3 ft** above any operable window or air intake.
- Increase to full size before passing through the roof in cold climates to prevent frost closure.

### Pro Tips

- A gurgling drain or trap that loses its seal almost always means a **venting failure** — check developed length first.
- Floor drains in rarely-used areas need **trap primers** (Sioux Chief) to keep the seal from evaporating.
- Keep horizontal vent runs above the flood-level rim of the fixtures they serve.

title: Backflow Prevention and Pressure Regulation: Protecting the Potable System
content:
## Backflow Prevention and PRV Best Practices

Protecting the potable supply from contamination and controlling pressure are non-negotiable. Cross-connections can siphon contaminants into drinking water; excess pressure destroys fixtures and causes water hammer.

### Pressure Reduction (PRV)

Code caps fixture pressure at **80 PSI**. Many municipal mains run 90-150 PSI.

- Install a **Watts LFN45B** or **Watts U5B** PRV on the main after the meter and main shutoff.
- Set to **50-60 PSI** for comfort and fixture longevity; verify with a gauge on a hose bib.
- A PRV creates a **closed system**, which mandates a **thermal expansion tank** at the water heater — without it, expanding hot water spikes pressure and pops the T&P valve.

### Backflow Assemblies (by hazard)

- **Atmospheric Vacuum Breaker (AVB):** Hose bibs, irrigation zones — simplest, no continuous pressure.
- **Pressure Vacuum Breaker (PVB):** Lawn irrigation under continuous pressure; install 12" above highest head.
- **Double Check Valve Assembly (DCVA):** Low-hazard cross-connections (fire lines without chemicals).
- **Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ):** **Watts 909** or **Zurn Wilkins 975XL** — required for **high-hazard** connections (boilers with chemicals, commercial, irrigation with fertigation). Has a relief port that dumps water if it fails — needs an air gap to drain.

### Install & Test Best Practices

1. Install RPZ/PVB with required clearances and an approved drain for relief discharge.
2. **Backflow assemblies must be tested at installation and annually** by a certified tester with a calibrated test kit.
3. Provide shutoffs upstream and downstream and test cocks.
4. Protect outdoor assemblies from freezing — RPZs are not freeze-tolerant.

### Common Cross-Connection Hazards

- Hose-end sprayers/chemicals (use a vacuum breaker on every hose bib).
- Boiler make-up water, commercial dish/laundry, irrigation, fire systems.

### Pro Tips

- Pair the **Watts PRV** with a Watts expansion tank pre-charged to match the set PSI.
- Install a `pressure gauge` permanently at the PRV for quick diagnosis.
- Keep an air gap between the RPZ relief port and the drain — direct connection is a code violation.
- Document the assembly serial number and test results for the local water authority.

title: Diagnosing Low Water Pressure, Water Hammer, and Running Toilets
content:
## Field Troubleshooting: Pressure, Hammer, and Toilets

These three complaints make up a large share of residential service calls. Systematic diagnosis beats parts-cannon guessing.

### Low Water Pressure

Start by measuring actual static pressure at a hose bib with a gauge.

- **Whole-house low:**
  - Check the **PRV** — a failing **Watts** PRV diaphragm drops downstream pressure. Adjust or rebuild.
  - Partially closed main or meter valve.
  - Clogged whole-house filter or galvanized pipe corrosion (replace galvanized with PEX/copper).
- **Single fixture low:**
  - Clean the **aerator** (Moen/Delta) — mineral buildup is the #1 cause.
  - Clogged showerhead or restricted **angle-stop**.
  - Cartridge debris on **Moen Posi-Temp** / **Delta** valves.
- **Hot only low:** Sediment in the water heater or a partially closed isolation valve; clogged tankless inlet screen.

### Water Hammer

That bang when a valve/appliance closes fast is a pressure shockwave.

1. Verify pressure isn't above **80 PSI** — install/adjust a Watts PRV.
2. Install **mechanical water-hammer arrestors** (Sioux Chief MiniRester) at washing machine and dishwasher quick-closing solenoid valves — the most common culprits.
3. Re-charge old **air chambers** (shut off water, drain system, let air back in).
4. Secure loose pipes with cushioned clamps — banging pipe against framing amplifies noise.

### Running / Phantom-Flushing Toilet

A toilet that refills periodically or runs constantly is leaking from tank to bowl.

- **Flapper/seal:** Most common. Worn or warped flapper (Kohler/American Standard) won't seal — replace it. Dye-tablet test confirms tank-to-bowl leak.
- **Fill valve:** Failing fill valve (Fluidmaster 400A) overfills past the overflow tube — set water level 1" below tube top.
- **Flush valve seat:** Mineral-pitted seat won't seal even with a new flapper — replace the flush valve.
- **Refill tube** stuffed too far down the overflow siphons water — keep it above the waterline.

### Pro Tips

- Carry a `0-160 PSI` gauge — pressure is the root cause of hammer, leaks, and running fixtures more often than people expect.
- For chronic hammer at appliances, arrestors outperform re-charged air chambers, which waterlog over time.
- Replace whole rubber kits on older toilets rather than one part.
code_references: IPC 604.9 — water hammer arrestors required at quick-closing valves

title: Gas Line Safety: Sizing, Sediment Traps, Leak Testing, and Connectors
content:
## Fuel Gas Piping Safety and Best Practices

Gas work is unforgiving — leaks cause fires, explosions, and CO poisoning. Follow fuel-gas code (IFGC/NFPA 54) precisely and never improvise.

### Pipe Materials

- **Black iron (Schedule 40)** — standard for interior runs; never galvanized on the interior gas side per many jurisdictions due to flaking.
- **CSST (corrugated stainless, e.g., Gastite/TracPipe)** — fast install but **must be bonded/grounded** per manufacturer and NEC 250.104 to prevent lightning-induced arcing perforation. Use only arc-resistant CSST where required.
- **Approved connectors** — listed appliance connectors (IFGC 411); never use them through walls or concealed.

### Sizing

Size by **total connected BTU load**, longest run, and allowable pressure drop. Example: a 100,000 BTU furnace + 199,000 BTU tankless + 65,000 BTU range over a 60-ft run typically needs **1"** trunk reducing to branches — always verify with the IFGC sizing tables for the system pressure (7" WC standard or 2 PSI).

### Required Safety Components

- **Sediment trap (drip leg):** Required ahead of each appliance (IFGC 408.4) — a capped tee that catches debris/moisture before it reaches the gas valve.
- **Appliance shutoff valve:** Within 6 ft of and in the same room as the appliance.
- **Manifold/main shutoff:** Accessible.

### Leak Testing

1. **Pressure test new piping** at the code value — commonly **1.5x working pressure, minimum 3 PSI, held 10+ minutes** (local AHJ may require more, e.g., 10 PSI). Use a calibrated manometer/gauge, not soap alone.
2. After connecting appliances, **leak-check every joint** with bubble solution or an electronic gas detector — never an open flame.
3. Purge air from lines safely to outdoors before lighting.

### CO and Combustion Safety

- Confirm proper venting and combustion air for every appliance.
- Install **CO alarms** near sleeping areas.
- A yellow/lazy flame, soot, or a backdrafting water heater signals incomplete combustion — shut down and investigate.

### Pro Tips

- Apply gas-rated thread sealant (yellow PTFE tape rated for gas or pipe dope) — never standard white tape.
- Bond CSST with a #6 copper conductor to the grounding electrode system.
- Tag and document the test pressure and duration for inspection.
- If you smell gas: no switches, no flames — evacuate and shut off at the meter.

title: Manual J Load Calculation and Equipment Sizing Fundamentals
content:
## Sizing HVAC Equipment with Manual J and Manual S

Proper sizing is the single most important decision in an HVAC install. Oversized equipment short-cycles, fails to dehumidify, and wears out early. Undersized equipment can't hold setpoint on design days.

### Manual J — The Load Calculation

**ACCA Manual J** computes the home's heat gain (cooling) and heat loss (heating) in **BTU/hr** at design conditions. Inputs:

- **Design temperatures:** Use the **ACCA/ASHRAE 1% and 99% design temps** for your location (not record extremes).
- **Building envelope:** Wall/ceiling/floor R-values, window U-factor and SHGC, orientation.
- **Infiltration:** Tight vs. leaky construction (ACH).
- **Internal gains:** Occupants (~230 BTU/person sensible), appliances, lighting.
- **Duct losses** if in unconditioned space.

Rule-of-thumb "500 sq ft per ton" is **not acceptable** — it routinely oversizes by 30-50%.

### Converting Load to Tonnage

- **1 ton = 12,000 BTU/hr** of cooling.
- A 30,000 BTU/hr cooling load = **2.5 tons**.
- Typical right-sized homes: 1 ton per 600-1,000 sq ft depending on climate and envelope.

### Manual S — Equipment Selection

Manual S matches the Manual J load to actual equipment performance data:

- Cooling: size to **95-115%** of the sensible cooling load — do **not** round up a full ton.
- In humid climates, favor lower latent capacity ratios and variable-speed for dehumidification.
- Match condenser + coil + blower as an **AHRI-rated matched system** (e.g., **Carrier Infinity**, **Trane XV**, **Lennox SL** series) — mismatched coils void the rating.

### Manual D — Duct Design

Size ducts to the airflow (CFM) the equipment needs — typically **400 CFM/ton** for AC. A 3-ton system moves ~1,200 CFM.

### Pro Tips

- Run the calc in software (Wrightsoft, Cool Calc, or CoolCalc free tier) for code compliance — many jurisdictions now require a Manual J submittal.
- For variable-speed inverter equipment (**Carrier Greenspeed**, **Trane Variable Speed**, **Daikin Fit**), modest oversizing is more forgiving because they modulate down.
- Document window specs and insulation — they swing the load more than square footage.
- Heat pump sizing balances heating and cooling loads; size to cooling, add backup heat strips for the heating shortfall.
code_references: IRC M1401.3 — equipment sizing per ACCA Manual J
ACCA Manual J/S/D — residential load & equipment selection

title: Split-System AC Installation: Line Set, Brazing, and Evacuation
content:
## Installing a Residential Split-System Air Conditioner

A split system pairs an outdoor condenser with an indoor evaporator coil/air handler, linked by a refrigerant line set. Clean install practices determine reliability and efficiency.

### Equipment & Layout

- Match an AHRI-rated set: e.g., **Goodman GSXC** condenser + matched coil, or **Rheem/Ruud** Endeavor, **York** Affinity, **Lennox** Merit.
- Set the condenser on a composite pad, level, **12"+ clearance** on intake sides and **24"+** on the service side.
- Plan the **line set**: large insulated **suction line** and small **liquid line** (e.g., 3/4" suction × 3/8" liquid for a 3-ton — always verify the unit's spec).

### Line Set Installation

1. Route with gentle bends — kinks restrict flow. Keep total length and lift within the manufacturer's limits; add refrigerant per foot beyond the factory charge length (typically beyond 15 ft).
2. Insulate the suction line fully (closed-cell, 1/2"+ wall).
3. Keep ends capped until brazing to prevent moisture/debris.

### Brazing

- Use **15% silver-phosphorus (Sil-Fos)** rod on copper-to-copper joints; brazing alloy with silver for copper-to-brass.
- **Flow dry nitrogen** at low pressure through the line while brazing to prevent internal oxidation (scale that contaminates the system).
- Don't overheat service valves — wrap with a wet rag or use a heat block.

### Evacuation (Critical)

Moisture and non-condensables kill compressors.

1. Pressure-test with **dry nitrogen** to the high-side test pressure; hold and verify no drop.
2. Pull a deep vacuum to **≤ 500 microns** with a quality vacuum pump and a **micron gauge** (not the compound gauge).
3. **Decay test:** Isolate the pump; vacuum must hold below ~500-1000 microns for several minutes. A rising vacuum means a leak or moisture — fix before charging.

### Charging & Startup

- Release the factory charge (open service valves) for standard line lengths, then trim by **superheat/subcooling** (see charging article).
- Verify with **Fieldpiece** or **Yellow Jacket** manifold/probes.

### Electrical

- Dedicated breaker per nameplate MCA/MOCP; whip and disconnect within sight of the condenser.
- 18/5 thermostat wire to the air handler; confirm 24V control.

### Pro Tips

- Never use the system compressor to pull a vacuum.
- Label the charge added and final superheat/subcooling on the unit.
- A.O. quality install = nitrogen purge + 500-micron vacuum + proper charge. Skip any and you'll be back.

title: Refrigerant Charging by Superheat and Subcooling (R-410A and R-454B A2L)
content:
## Charging a System Correctly: Superheat and Subcooling

A system charged "by feel" or by gauge pressure alone is almost always wrong. Use **superheat** for fixed-orifice/piston metering and **subcooling** for TXV/EEV systems.

### The Two Methods

- **Superheat (fixed orifice):** Measured suction-line temperature minus the saturation temperature at suction pressure. Compare to the **target superheat** from the manufacturer's chart (function of indoor wet-bulb and outdoor dry-bulb). Low charge = high superheat; add refrigerant to bring it down.
- **Subcooling (TXV/EEV):** Saturation temperature at liquid pressure minus the actual liquid-line temperature. Most modern systems target **8-12°F subcooling** (verify nameplate). Low subcooling = undercharge; add refrigerant.

### Procedure

1. Run the system 15-20 minutes to stabilize; indoor airflow set correctly (~400 CFM/ton).
2. Connect **Fieldpiece** wireless probes or **Yellow Jacket** manifold; attach line-temp clamps.
3. Read suction and liquid saturation from the gauge's P/T scale for the **specific refrigerant**.
4. Calculate superheat or subcooling; compare to target.
5. Add refrigerant in small charges (vapor on the low side for blends) and re-stabilize between adjustments.

### Refrigerant Notes

- **R-410A** — current HFC standard; **non-flammable (A1)**. Charge as liquid (it's a near-azeotropic blend) metered into the low side.
- **R-454B (A2L)** — the EPA-mandated low-GWP replacement phasing in for new equipment (Carrier, Trane, Lennox, Daikin). **Mildly flammable (A2L)** — requires A2L-rated gauges, recovery machines, leak detectors, and adherence to charge limits and ventilation/spark-control practices.
- **Never mix refrigerants** or top off a contaminated system — recover, evacuate, and recharge to nameplate weight.

### A2L Safety Requirements

- Use **A2L-listed tools** and refrigerant detection where required (RDS sensors in equipment).
- No open flames or ignition sources near a charged A2L system during service.
- Ensure adequate ventilation; respect maximum charge per room volume.

### EPA 608 Compliance

- Technicians must hold **EPA 608 certification**.
- **Recover** refrigerant before opening a system; venting is illegal.
- Use a recovery machine and DOT-approved cylinders; track refrigerant.

### Pro Tips

- Weigh in the charge by scale on a fresh install (most accurate), then verify with subcooling.
- High subcooling + high head pressure = overcharge or condenser airflow problem.
- Record final superheat/subcooling, ambient, and added weight on the unit.

title: Ductwork Design and Static Pressure: Sizing for Airflow and Comfort
content:
## Duct Design and Static Pressure Best Practices

The best equipment fails behind bad ductwork. Restrictive ducts starve the blower, cause noise, freeze coils, and waste energy.

### Airflow Targets

- **AC:** ~**400 CFM per ton** (350-450 range). A 3-ton system needs ~1,200 CFM.
- **Furnace heating:** sized to the blower's rise range (e.g., 40-70°F temp rise on the nameplate).

### Static Pressure — The Vital Sign

Measure **Total External Static Pressure (TESP)** with a manometer at the supply and return plenums.

- Most residential equipment is rated at **0.5" w.c.** max TESP.
- Field reality: many systems run **0.8-1.2" w.c.** — dangerously high, choking airflow.
- High static causes high head pressure, low capacity, iced coils, and premature blower failure.

### Sizing with Manual D / Friction Rate

- Determine **Available Static Pressure (ASP)** = equipment max − component losses (coil, filter, registers, dampers).
- Compute a **friction rate** (typically **0.06-0.10 "w.c./100 ft**) and size trunks/branches off a ductulator or Manual D software.
- **Return air is usually the weak link** — undersized returns cause most high-static problems. Provide ample return area; aim for low return-grille face velocity (≤ 500 fpm).

### Materials & Fabrication

- **Sheet metal trunks** are best for performance; size per friction rate.
- **Flex duct** is acceptable for short branch runs — must be **pulled tight** (sagging flex can cut effective area in half) and supported every 4-5 ft.
- **Seal all joints with mastic** (UL 181) — not cloth duct tape. Seal to the metal, including the plenum and boots.
- Insulate ducts in unconditioned space to **R-8**.

### Filtration

- A clean filter with adequate face area is essential — a 4" media filter (e.g., Honeywell/Aprilaire) flows far better than a 1" pleated filter and lasts longer. Size to keep velocity under ~300 fpm.

### Pro Tips

- Always **measure TESP** on every install and service — it's the HVAC equivalent of blood pressure.
- Balance the system with adjustable dampers; set airflow per room to the Manual J loads.
- Avoid sharp 90s and undersized return grilles; use turning vanes in square elbows.
- Verify temperature rise/split after duct work to confirm airflow is in spec.

title: Ductless Mini-Split Installation: Mounting, Line Set, and Commissioning
content:
## Installing a Ductless Mini-Split Heat Pump

Mini-splits deliver zoned, high-efficiency heating and cooling without ductwork. Quality leaders include **Mitsubishi Electric (Mr. Slim / M-Series)**, **Fujitsu (Halcyon)**, and **Daikin**.

### Equipment & Sizing

- Size each indoor head to the **room's** Manual J load — don't oversize; mini-splits modulate but still need correct capacity for dehumidification.
- Common single-zone units: **9k, 12k, 18k, 24k BTU**. Multi-zone outdoor units (e.g., Mitsubishi MXZ) serve several heads.
- Cold-climate variants (Mitsubishi **Hyper-Heat / H2i**, Fujitsu XLTH) deliver rated heat down to **-13°F to -15°F**.

### Indoor Head Mounting

1. Mount the wall bracket level, high on an exterior wall, with clearance above/below per the manual.
2. Bore a **~3" (65-80mm)** wall penetration, sloped slightly downward to the exterior for condensate drainage.
3. Route the bundled line set, control wire, and condensate drain through the sleeve.

### Line Set & Connections

- Mini-splits use **flare connections** (not brazed) at both ends — typically **1/4" liquid × 3/8" or 1/2" suction**.
- Cut tubing square, deburr **facing down**, and make clean **45° flares** with a quality flaring tool. Apply a drop of refrigerant oil; torque flare nuts to the **manufacturer's spec** (over-torquing cracks flares — a leading failure point).
- Keep within the max line length and lift; add refrigerant per foot beyond the pre-charge length.

### Outdoor Unit

- Wall bracket or ground pad, level, with service clearance and lifted above snow line.
- Dedicated circuit per nameplate; connect interconnecting control cable matching terminal numbers exactly.

### Evacuation & Startup

1. Pressure-test the field flares with **dry nitrogen**.
2. Pull vacuum to **≤ 500 microns** with a micron gauge; decay test.
3. Open the **service valve stems** to release the factory charge.
4. Power up; run in cooling and heating; verify head delta-T and no flare leaks (electronic detector + bubbles).

### Condensate

- Slope the drain line continuously; on below-grade or interior heads use a **condensate pump** if gravity drainage isn't possible.

### Pro Tips

- Most mini-split callbacks are **flare leaks** — use a torque wrench, not feel.
- Vacuum to 500 microns; the small charge is unforgiving of moisture.
- Insulate both line-set lines fully; UV-protect exterior insulation with line-hide.
materials_required: Mitsubishi Mr. Slim head + MXZ/MUZ condenser

title: Gas Furnace Installation: Venting, Combustion Air, and Condensate
content:
## Installing a Gas Furnace Correctly and Safely

A gas furnace install ties together gas, electrical, venting, ductwork, and (for condensing units) condensate. Efficiency category determines the venting approach.

### Furnace Categories

- **80% AFUE (Category I):** Naturally drafted/induced-draft, vents hot flue gas through **Type B double-wall vent** or a metal chimney liner — must slope **up** and stay warm to draft.
- **90%+ AFUE condensing (Category IV):** Sealed combustion, **PVC/CPVC** intake and exhaust, produces acidic condensate. Leaders: **Carrier Infinity 59**, **Trane S9V2**, **Lennox SLP99V**, **Goodman GMVC**, **Rheem/Ruud** R96V.

### Sizing & Placement

- Size by **Manual J** heating load; match blower CFM to the AC tonnage.
- Set level on the platform with proper clearances to combustibles per the nameplate.
- Orientation: upflow, downflow, or horizontal — configure the unit accordingly.

### Venting (Condensing, Category IV)

- **2" or 3" PVC** intake and exhaust sized per the vent tables (diameter depends on input BTU and equivalent length).
- Maintain max equivalent vent length and minimum/maximum elbow counts.
- **Termination clearances:** Exhaust min **12"** above grade/snow line, **12"** from the intake (or use a concentric kit), and **4 ft** from windows/doors and gas meters; keep 3 ft from inside corners per manufacturer detail.
- Slope exhaust back to the furnace so condensate drains to the trap.

### Combustion Air

- Sealed-combustion units pull intake air through the dedicated pipe — best practice.
- Atmospheric units in confined spaces need **two openings** (high and low) sized to the BTU load and the space (e.g., 1 sq in per 1,000 BTU/hr from outdoors).

### Gas & Electrical

- Gas line sized to input BTU with a **sediment trap (drip leg)** and shutoff within 6 ft.
- Set **manifold pressure** (typically **3.5" WC for NG**) and verify input by clocking the meter.
- Dedicated 120V circuit; 24V thermostat wiring.

### Condensate

- Route through the unit's trap to a drain via a **neutralizer** (acidic, pH ~3). Add a condensate pump if no gravity drain.

### Commissioning

1. Leak-test gas; bubble-check all joints.
2. Start and run a **combustion analysis** — verify CO (< 100 ppm air-free), O2, and stack temp.
3. Confirm **temperature rise** is within the nameplate range; adjust blower speed.
4. Test all safeties: rollout switch, limit, pressure switch, flame sensor.

### Pro Tips

- Always run a combustion analyzer — eyeballing the flame isn't commissioning.
- A clean flame sensor prevents the most common no-heat callback.
- Verify the condensate trap is primed; a dry/clogged trap trips the pressure switch.

title: Thermostat and Zoning Wiring: From R/C/W/Y/G to Multi-Stage Heat Pumps
content:
## Wiring Thermostats and Zone Control Systems

Thermostat miswiring is a top cause of no-heat/no-cool calls and fried control boards. Know the standard terminals and the equipment behind them.

### Standard 24V Terminal Map

- **R / Rc / Rh** — 24V power (Rc cooling, Rh heating; jumper if single transformer).
- **C** — common (24V return) — **required** for Wi-Fi stats (**Ecobee**, **Nest**, **Honeywell T-series**) to power themselves.
- **W / W2** — heat stage 1 / stage 2.
- **Y / Y2** — compressor/cooling stage 1 / stage 2.
- **G** — indoor fan/blower.
- **O/B** — heat pump reversing valve (**O** energized in cooling = most brands; **B** energized in heating = Rheem/Ruud).
- **AUX/E** — auxiliary/emergency heat (heat strips on heat pumps).

### Common Configurations

- **Conventional AC + gas furnace:** R, C, W, Y, G (+ Y2/W2 for two-stage).
- **Heat pump:** R, C, Y, G, O/B, plus **AUX** and **E** for backup heat. Set the thermostat to heat-pump mode and correct O/B logic.
- **Dual-fuel (heat pump + gas furnace):** Needs a thermostat that supports a **balance point** to switch from compressor to gas below a set outdoor temp.

### The C-Wire Issue

No C-wire? Options: run a new conductor, repurpose an unused wire, or use a **Fast-Stat / add-a-wire** adapter. Nest's power-stealing can cause intermittent faults on some systems — a true C is best practice.

### Zoning Systems

Zoning uses a **control panel** (Honeywell TrueZone, Ecobee SmartSensor logic, or panel-based) driving **motorized dampers** per zone.

- Each zone gets its own thermostat feeding the panel.
- The panel manages dampers and staging, and uses a **bypass damper or modulating/variable-speed equipment** to relieve static when only one zone calls.
- Best paired with **variable-speed/inverter** equipment (Carrier Greenspeed, Trane) so airflow modulates instead of dumping into a bypass.

### Commissioning

1. Power off at the disconnect before wiring.
2. Match wires to terminals; configure stat for the equipment type and stages.
3. Test each call: G (fan), Y (cool), W (heat), AUX/E, and O/B reversing.
4. Verify damper operation per zone and confirm static stays in range.

### Pro Tips

- Always land a **C-wire** on smart stats — it eliminates power-stealing gremlins.
- Label wires before pulling the old stat; photograph the terminals.
- Wrong O/B setting = heating when you want cooling — verify reversing-valve logic per brand.

title: Diagnosing Low Cooling, Frozen Coils, and No-Heat Calls
content:
## Systematic HVAC Troubleshooting

Three of the most common service calls — weak cooling, iced coils, and no heat — share overlapping root causes. Diagnose with measurements, not guesses.

### Low / Weak Cooling

Measure the **temperature split** (return-air temp minus supply-air temp) — should be **16-22°F** at the coil under normal humidity.

- **Low refrigerant charge:** High superheat, low subcooling, low suction pressure — find and fix the **leak** (electronic detector/bubbles), recover, repair, evacuate, recharge to spec. Never just top off.
- **Dirty condenser coil:** High head pressure, hot condenser — wash with coil cleaner.
- **Restricted airflow:** Dirty filter/evaporator, high static — clean, fix ductwork.
- **Failing compressor/capacitor:** Test the **run capacitor** (within ±6% of rated µF) and compressor amps vs. RLA.
- **Metering device (TXV)** stuck — erratic superheat.

### Frozen Evaporator Coil

Ice forms when coil temp drops below freezing — almost always **airflow or charge**.

1. **Low airflow** (most common): dirty filter, dirty coil, undersized/blocked returns, weak blower, closed dampers. Restore airflow.
2. **Low refrigerant charge:** undercharge drops suction pressure/coil temp below freezing.
3. **Low ambient operation** or stuck blower relay.

**Fix steps:** Shut off cooling, run **fan-only to thaw** completely, then diagnose the root cause before restarting — don't just restart into another freeze.

### No Heat (Gas Furnace)

Follow the ignition sequence with a meter:

1. **Call for heat:** 24V at W? If not, check thermostat/C-wire/transformer (3A fuse on board).
2. **Inducer runs?** No → bad inducer or board.
3. **Pressure switch closes?** Check for blocked vent/intake or **clogged condensate trap** (condensing units trip the switch).
4. **Igniter glows / spark?** Cracked **hot surface igniter** is common — test resistance (~40-90Ω).
5. **Gas valve opens / flame?** Verify gas on, manifold pressure.
6. **Flame sense:** Weak/dirty **flame sensor** = furnace lights then drops out after a few seconds (microamp reading too low). Clean it — the #1 no-heat fix.
7. **Limit switch open** from overheating → check airflow.

### No Heat (Heat Pump)

- Verify reversing-valve **O/B** logic, defrost board, and that **AUX heat strips** energize. Check for iced outdoor coil (failed defrost).

### Pro Tips

- Carry a **multimeter, manometer, and gauges** — measure don't guess.
- A clean flame sensor and clean filter resolve a huge share of calls.
- Always find the leak before recharging — refrigerant doesn't disappear on its own.

title: Refrigerant and Carbon Monoxide Safety: A2L Handling and Combustion Hazards
content:
## Refrigerant and CO Safety on the Job

HVAC techs work around asphyxiants, flammable refrigerants, high pressure, and combustion byproducts. These hazards are invisible — respect them.

### Refrigerant Hazards

- **Asphyxiation:** Refrigerants displace oxygen in low areas (basements, pits). Ventilate; never service in unventilated confined spaces.
- **Frostbite:** Liquid refrigerant boils at sub-zero temps — wear **safety glasses and gloves**; flares and connections can spray.
- **High pressure:** R-410A operates ~400+ PSI on the high side and far higher under fault; R-454B is similar. Use **rated gauges/hoses**, never overheat a charged cylinder, and never exceed cylinder fill limits.

### A2L (R-454B / R-32) Flammability

New low-GWP refrigerants are **mildly flammable (A2L class)**:

- Use **A2L-rated** recovery machines, gauges, vacuum pumps, and **leak detectors**.
- **No ignition sources** — no smoking, no open flame, no sparking tools near a charged/leaking A2L system.
- Equipment may include **refrigerant detection sensors (RDS)** that trigger fans — don't defeat them.
- Respect **maximum charge per room volume** limits and ensure ventilation.
- Brazing on an A2L system: recover fully, then purge with nitrogen before applying heat.

### EPA 608 / Legal

- **Venting refrigerant is illegal** (Clean Air Act §608). **Recover** before opening systems.
- Hold **EPA 608 certification**; use DOT-approved recovery cylinders and track refrigerant.

### Carbon Monoxide (Combustion Side)

CO is colorless, odorless, and deadly. Sources: cracked heat exchangers, backdrafting furnaces/water heaters, blocked flues.

- **Always run a combustion analysis** on furnace startup/service — target **CO air-free < 100 ppm**, ideally near zero; investigate anything elevated.
- Inspect the **heat exchanger** for cracks — a leaking exchanger sends CO into the supply air. Shut down and red-tag if cracked.
- Verify proper **draft** and that vent/flue is clear and correctly sloped.
- Install/test **CO alarms** near sleeping areas; recommend low-level CO monitors for clients.

### Electrical & General

- **Lock out/tag out** at the disconnect before servicing; verify 0V with a meter.
- Discharge **run/start capacitors** before handling — they hold a shock charge.
- Watch for spinning condenser fans and hot surfaces.

### Pro Tips

- Keep a **personal CO monitor** clipped on during combustion work.
- Transition to A2L tools now — new equipment is shipping with R-454B.
- If a customer reports headaches/nausea that improve when they leave home, treat it as a CO emergency.

title: Wall Framing Layout: Plate Marking and Stud Spacing at 16" and 24" OC
content:
## Wall Framing Layout

Accurate layout is what separates a wall that drywalls and sheathes clean from one that fights you every panel. Start by snapping chalk lines on the slab or subfloor to locate the **inside edge** of the bottom plate per the floor plan.

### Plating and Crowning

Cut your top and bottom plates from straight `2x4` or `2x6` SPF/DF #2 stock. Lay them edge-to-edge (this is **ganging the plates**) so you mark both at once. Always frame exterior walls in DF #2 or SPF #2 — crown every stud and orient crowns up consistently.

### On-Center Spacing

- **16" OC** is standard for load-bearing walls and walls receiving `1/2"` drywall on ceilings/walls per **IRC R602.3(5)**.
- **24" OC** is allowed for many non-bearing and single-story bearing walls with `2x6` studs (advanced framing / OVE), saving lumber and improving insulation cavity.
- Pull your tape and mark **15-1/4"** for the first stud center so the leading edge of the first `4x8` sheet of sheathing lands on stud center at 16". Mark with an **X** on the side the stud sits. Continue at 16" increments: 31-1/4", 47-1/4", etc.

### Openings

Mark king studs, then trimmers (jack studs), then the rough opening. Standard interior door RO is door width + 2" for jamb/shim. Use a **Speed Square** and a sharp pencil or a **DeWalt** layout marker.

### Assembly

- Nail through the plate into the stud end with **2) 16d** nails (`3-1/2"`) per **IRC R602.3(1)** — end nail, 2 each end.
- A **Paslode** or **Hitachi/Metabo HPT** framing nailer with 3-1/4" paper-collated nails speeds this dramatically.
- Stand the wall, plumb it, and brace with `1x4` or `2x4` diagonals before releasing.

### Pro Tips

- Keep layout consistent across the whole floor so plumbing/electrical and HVAC stack between bays.
- Mark **C** for cripples and **T** for trimmers to avoid confusion.
- Double-check your **first stud offset** — getting it wrong throws every sheet of sheathing and drywall off module.

A disciplined layout pays off through the entire build: sheathing, drywall, and trim all reference the same 16" module, so panels break on framing and fasteners land where they should.

title: Header Sizing and Spans for Bearing and Non-Bearing Walls
content:
## Header Sizing and Spans

Headers carry roof, floor, and wall loads across openings. Undersizing causes sag, drywall cracking, and sticking doors. Size from **IRC Table R602.7(1)** for exterior bearing walls and **R602.7(2)** for interior bearing walls, or use engineered lumber tables.

### Sawn Lumber Headers

Common built-up headers use two or three `2x` members with `1/2"` plywood spacer to fill a 3-1/2" stud bay (a `2x` is 1-1/2" thick; 2 plies + 1/2" ply = 3-1/2").

- **(2) 2x6 DF #2**: spans roughly **4'-0"** supporting roof + ceiling, one story.
- **(2) 2x8**: approx **5'-0"** to **6'-0"** depending on building width and snow load.
- **(2) 2x10**: approx **6'-6"** to **8'-0"**.
- **(2) 2x12**: approx **8'-0"** to **9'-6"**.

Spans drop as building width (20', 28', 36') and ground snow load increase — always check the actual table column.

### Engineered Lumber Headers

For longer or heavily loaded spans, use **Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist Microllam LVL** (1.55E or 2.0E) or **Parallam PSL**. A `(2) 1-3/4" x 11-7/8" Microllam LVL` header readily spans garage door openings of **9'-16'** depending on load. **Boise Cascade VERSA-LAM** LVL is an equivalent product. Always defer to the manufacturer span tables or an engineer for garage and great-room beams.

### Jack and King Studs

The number of **jack (trimmer) studs** per side increases with span/load — `1` jack for short openings, `2-3` jacks for wide LVL headers per the manufacturer detail. **IRC Table R602.7.5** gives minimum jack/king counts.

### Connections

- Nail built-up sawn headers per **IRC R602.3(1)**: 16d at 16" OC each edge, staggered top and bottom.
- For multi-ply LVL/PSL, follow the **Trus Joist** nailing/bolting schedule (e.g., 2 rows 16d at 12" OC, or `1/2"` through-bolts at 24" OC for 3+ plies and side-loaded conditions). **GRK RSS** structural screws are an approved alternative to nails for many multi-ply built-ups — check the connector and beam manufacturer details.
- Use **Simpson Strong-Tie** column caps (**CC/ECC** series) or face-mount hangers (**HUC/HGUS**) where beams frame into posts or carry girder loads.

### Header Bearing and Cripples

- Provide full bearing under each header end onto the jack studs; crush at the bearing point signals an undersized condition.
- Above the header, fill with **cripple studs** at the same OC as the wall studs to carry the top-plate load down to the header.
- A continuous **rim/band** over the opening keeps the top plate aligned.

### Key Rule

Non-bearing interior walls can use a flat `2x4` or single `2x6` header for openings up to ~8'. Never assume bearing vs. non-bearing from the floor plan alone — verify the **load path** from roof and floors all the way to the foundation before sizing. When in doubt on garage beams, great rooms, or anything carrying a girder truss, get a **stamped engineered design** rather than guessing from a span table.

title: Floor Joist and TJI Layout: Spans, Spacing, and Squash Blocks
content:
## Floor Joist and TJI Layout

Floor systems must meet **L/360** live-load deflection for finished floors. Layout drives squeak-free, flat floors.

### Sawn Joist Spans

From **IRC Table R502.3.1(2)** (40 psf live, 10 psf dead, #2 grade):
- `2x8 DF #2 @ 16" OC`: ~ **12'-7"**
- `2x10 DF #2 @ 16" OC`: ~ **15'-5"**
- `2x12 DF #2 @ 16" OC`: ~ **18'-0"**

Going to 24" OC or southern pine/SPF changes spans — verify the species column.

### Engineered I-Joists (TJI)

**Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist TJI** joists outperform sawn lumber for long, flat, quiet floors. Common series: **TJI 110, 210, 230, 360, 560**. A `TJI 230 @ 16" OC, 11-7/8" deep` spans roughly **17'-19'** at residential floor loading. Deeper `16"` TJIs reach well past **24'**. **Boise Cascade BCI** joists are a direct alternative.

### Critical TJI Rules

- **Never cut, notch, or drill the flanges.** Web holes only, per the manufacturer hole chart.
- Install **web stiffeners** (filler blocks) at hangers and concentrated loads where the detail requires.
- Use **squash blocks** (1-1/16" taller than the TJI) beside the joist under bearing walls/posts to carry vertical load around the I-joist — the flange alone won't take point loads.
- Provide **rim board** (Weyerhaeuser TimberStrand LSL rim, `1-1/4"` min) at all ends for lateral support and load transfer.
- Use approved hangers — **Simpson Strong-Tie ITT/IUS** series face-mount hangers sized to the I-joist, or **MiTek/USP** equivalents.

### Layout Procedure

1. Lay out rim/plate at **16" OC** matching wall studs above for stacked framing.
2. Set joists crown-up (sawn) — TJIs have no crown.
3. Glue and nail the subfloor — `3/4" T&G` Advantech with **PL Premium** construction adhesive and `2-3/8"` ring-shank nails or screws at 6" edge / 12" field.
4. Block at supports; add bridging/strongbacks for long spans to reduce bounce.

### Deflection and Bounce

Meeting the span table satisfies strength and **L/360** deflection, but occupants notice **vibration** long before structural limits. For long open floors, add a **TJI strongback** (a `2x6` on edge through the web knockouts mid-span) or tighten spacing to **12" OC** or **19.2" OC**. A stiffer subfloor (`23/32"`–`7/8"` Advantech) and full glue coverage also reduce perceived bounce.

### Bottom Line

Follow the **Weyerhaeuser Trus Joist Specifier's Guide** for hole locations, hanger selection, web stiffeners, squash blocks, and blocking — engineered floors are only as good as their details. Mixing a sawn rim with TJIs, point-loading a flange, or skipping squash blocks under a bearing wall are the failures that produce sagging floors and callbacks.

title: Selecting and Nailing Simpson Strong-Tie Connectors
content:
## Simpson Strong-Tie Connector Selection and Nailing

Connectors only achieve their rated load when you install **every specified fastener** in **every hole** with the **correct nail**. The most common field failure is short nails or empty holes.

### Joist Hangers

- **LUS28** — face-mount hanger for a single `2x8`. **LUS26**, **LUS210** size to 2x6/2x10. Fill round joist holes and the double-shear angled holes.
- Use **10d x 1-1/2" (N10)** joist nails into the joist and **16d (N16)** into the header where the table calls for them. Do not substitute drywall or deck screws.
- For I-joists use **ITT/IUS/MIU** series; for heavy beams use **HUC/HGUS** concealed/heavy hangers.

### Hurricane/Seismic Ties

- **H2.5A** and **H1** ties tie rafters/trusses to the top plate to resist uplift. Install per the truss-to-plate connection schedule, typically **5) 8d x 1-1/2"** each.
- **LSTA21 / LSTA24 / MSTA** strap ties splice plates and provide continuity across openings.

### Hold-Downs

- **HDU** series (HDU2, HDU5, HDU8, HDU11) bolt to a post and anchor to a **Simpson SSTB or PAB anchor bolt** in the foundation for shear-wall overturning. Use the specified **SDS screws** (e.g., HDU5 = 14) **SDS25300**) into the post and torque the anchor nut to spec.
- **PHD/HD** bolted hold-downs are used for heavier conditions.

### Fastener Discipline

- Simpson connectors are designed for **Simpson Strong-Drive SD/SDS structural screws** or specified common nails. **GRK RSS/structural screws** are excellent for general structural fastening but use Simpson-approved fasteners in Simpson connectors.
- **MiTek/USP** offers cross-referenced equivalents — do not mix a USP hanger with Simpson load values.
- Galvanize/stainless (**ZMAX / HDG**) in exterior, treated-lumber, or coastal conditions — ACQ pressure-treated lumber is corrosive to standard zinc.

### Post Bases and Caps

- **ABU/ABA** adjustable post bases and **CBSQ** column bases hold posts off concrete (1" standoff) to prevent rot and anchor to the foundation. **BC/BCS** post caps tie posts to beams.
- Match the base to the post size (`4x4`, `6x6`) and the anchor to the concrete (cast-in **PAB** or post-installed **Titen HD**).

### Verification

Use a connector that is **fully nailed off** — an inspector counts holes. A `LUS28` with two empty nail holes can lose a significant fraction of its rated capacity. **Fill them all** with the **correct length and diameter** fastener. Common red-tags: drywall/deck screws in hangers, 1-1/4" roofing nails where N10 joist nails are required, short nails that don't penetrate the supporting member, and skipped double-shear angle nails. Keep the **Simpson Strong-Tie connector catalog** or app on site to confirm the fastening schedule for each model before you hang it.

title: Wall Sheathing and Nailing Schedules per IRC R602.3
content:
## Wall Sheathing and Nailing Schedules

Structural wood sheathing braces walls against wind and seismic racking. The **nailing schedule** is the difference between a code-compliant shear panel and a wall that fails.

### Panel Selection

- **7/16" OSB** (APA rated, e.g., **LP**, **Weyerhaeuser**, **Norbord**) is the standard exterior wall sheathing. `15/32"` (1/2") plywood is used where higher capacity or moisture durability is needed.
- Orient panels with the strength axis (long dimension) across studs; stagger vertical joints.
- Leave a **1/8" gap** at panel edges and ends for expansion (use a nail or spacer tool).

### Standard Nailing — IRC Table R602.3(3)

For `3/8"`–`1/2"` wood structural panels on walls:
- **8d common (0.131" x 2-1/2")** nails
- **6" OC at panel edges**, **12" OC in the field** (intermediate supports).
- Keep nails **3/8" from panel edges** to avoid blowout.

### Braced Wall / Shear Wall Nailing

For engineered shear walls, the schedule tightens dramatically:
- **6" / 4" / 3" / 2" OC** edge nailing increases shear capacity per the engineer's schedule.
- Use **blocking** at all horizontal panel joints when the design calls for blocked shear walls.
- Mark the shear-wall schedule on the panel so the inspector and crew can verify.

### Tools and Pressure

- A **Hitachi/Metabo HPT NR83A5**, **Paslode**, or **Senco** framing nailer set to flush — **do not overdrive**. Nails countersunk past the OSB face lose shear value. Set depth on a scrap and adjust regulator (~90-100 psi).
- Hand-nail or palm-nail the last row where the gun can't reach flush.

### Continuous Load Path

Sheathing ties studs to the top and bottom plates and, with proper nailing into the **rim/sill**, transfers shear to the foundation. Combine with **Simpson** anchor bolts, hold-downs, and **mudsill anchors** for a complete braced-wall line per **IRC R602.10**.

### Panel Layout

- Run the first course with the bottom edge lapping the **mudsill/rim** so sheathing ties the wall to the foundation — this is critical to the braced-wall load path.
- Stagger vertical end joints by at least one stud bay between courses (running-bond pattern) for better diaphragm action.
- Block all unsupported horizontal joints when the shear schedule requires **blocked panels**; many engineered designs do.

### Quick Reference

- Field nailing forgotten? It's the most common red-tag — **12" OC in the field is mandatory**, not optional.
- **Over-driven nails** (sunk past the OSB face) and **edge blowout** both reduce shear capacity — set the gun on a scrap first and keep nails 3/8" from edges.
- A **WRB** (weather-resistive barrier such as **Tyvek HomeWrap** or **CertainTeed**) goes over the sheathing, lapped shingle-style, with all windows, doors, and penetrations flashed and integrated.
- For shear walls, **photograph and mark** the panel with its nailing schedule so both the crew and inspector can verify edge spacing at a glance.
code_references: IRC R602.3(3) — wood structural panel nailing

title: Diagnosing Squeaky Floors and Racking Walls
content:
## Troubleshooting Squeaks and Racking

### Squeaky Floors

Squeaks come from wood moving against a fastener or against another piece of wood. Common causes:
- **Subfloor not glued** to joists — nails work loose as lumber dries and the panel rubs the nail shank.
- **Smooth-shank nails** instead of ring-shank or screws backing out.
- **Gaps** between subfloor and joist (crowned or twisted joists) leaving the panel unsupported.

**Fixes:**
- From below: drive a **GRK or Simpson SDS screw** up through a `2x` cleat snugged tight under the subfloor where the gap exists. Do **not** pull the subfloor down onto a joist if a gap exists at a different joist — shim first.
- From above (finished): use a **Squeeeeak No More** scored-screw kit through carpet, or face-screw with **trim-head screws** into joists, then fill.
- New construction: always **glue** subfloor with **PL Premium** and fasten with ring-shank nails or subfloor screws at **6" edge / 12" field**. Use `3/4" Advantech` for dimensional stability.

### Racking and Out-of-Square Walls

Racking is lateral lozenging of a wall, usually from inadequate bracing during or after construction.
- **During framing:** walls left un-sheathed and un-braced rack in wind. Always install temporary `1x4` let-in or `2x4` diagonal bracing until sheathing is on.
- **Permanent:** racking resistance comes from **wood structural panel sheathing** nailed per **IRC R602.3(3)** or engineered shear walls per **R602.10**. Metal **let-in T-bracing** or Simpson **WB/RCWB** portal frames are alternatives.

**Diagnosis:**
- Measure diagonals corner-to-corner; equal diagonals = square. A difference indicates racking.
- Check **drywall cracks at door corners** and **sticking doors** as symptoms of seasonal racking or header sag.
- Verify **hold-downs (HDU)** and **anchor bolts** are present and tight at braced-wall ends — missing overturning restraint lets shear walls rotate.

### Twisted and Crowned Lumber

Green dimensional lumber moves as it dries. A twisted joist or a crowned-down member leaves the subfloor unsupported and creates squeaks and uneven floors.
- Always install joists and studs **crown up** and consistent.
- Block and bridge long joist spans to keep members from rolling/twisting.
- For chronic movement, switch to **engineered lumber (TJI, LSL studs)** which stays straight and stable.

### Prevention

Glue + screw subfloors with **PL Premium** and ring-shank or subfloor screws, fully nail sheathing per the schedule, brace walls until sheathed, and confirm the **continuous load path** from roof to foundation including hold-downs and anchor bolts. Let framing **dry/acclimate** before drywall to minimize shrinkage-driven cracks and pops. Most callbacks — squeaks, racking, cracked drywall corners, sticking doors — trace back to a single skipped fastening, bracing, or moisture-management step, so build the discipline in from the first wall.
materials_required: GRK or Simpson SDS structural screws

title: Ladder, Scaffold, and Fall Protection on the Frame
content:
## Fall Protection While Framing

Falls are the leading cause of death in construction. **OSHA 1926.501** requires fall protection at **6 feet** in residential construction. Plan it before you leave the ground.

### Ladders

- Maintain the **4:1 ratio** — base out 1 foot for every 4 feet of height.
- Extension ladders must extend **3 feet (3 rungs)** above the landing and be tied off at the top.
- Inspect for cracked rails, bent rungs; use **Type IA (300 lb)** rated ladders for framing loads (tools + body).
- Never stand on the top two rungs of a stepladder. Keep **three points of contact**.

### Scaffold and Pump Jacks

- Fully plank platforms; provide **guardrails at 39"-45"** with mid-rails when 10+ feet (or 6 ft for some scaffolds), and **toe boards**.
- Base plates and mud sills on firm, level ground; plumb and brace frames.
- Pump-jack poles must be braced to the wall every 10 feet.

### Personal Fall Arrest (PFAS)

Where guardrails aren't feasible at heights ≥6 ft (roofs, walls, openings):
- **Full-body harness** + **shock-absorbing lanyard or SRL** + anchor rated **5,000 lb** per worker.
- Use a **roof anchor** (e.g., **Guardian**, **Malta Dynamics**, **DBI-SALA**) screwed into rafters/trusses with the specified lag/structural screws.
- Calculate **total fall clearance** — free fall + deceleration + harness stretch + safety margin — so you don't strike a lower level.

### Floor and Wall Openings

- Cover floor holes with secured, marked covers rated for **2x the load**.
- Stair openings, shaftways, and skylights get guardrails or covers immediately after framing.

### Nailer and Saw Safety

- Sequential-trip triggers reduce double-fire injuries on **Paslode/Senco** guns. Keep the nailer pointed downrange; disconnect air before clearing jams.
- Eye and ear protection always; the **DeWalt** or **Makita** worm-drive saw demands guards intact and full attention.

### Working at the Wall and Eave

- When standing walls, keep crew clear of the swing path and brace immediately; an unbraced wall can topple in a gust.
- Setting trusses and rafters at the eave is high-exposure work — use a **harness tied to a roof anchor**, a **scaffold at the eave**, or a guardrailed work platform. Plan anchor points before the first truss flies.
- Cover or guard the **stair opening and floor openings** the moment the deck is sheeted.

### Housekeeping and Daily Routine

Clear cut-offs, coil cords and air hoses out of walk paths, and pick up spent nail strips and collation paper. A clean deck prevents the trips that turn into falls from height. Conduct a **daily inspection** of ladders, scaffolds, harnesses, lanyards, and anchors — tag out anything damaged. **Document** the inspection and hold a brief toolbox talk; OSHA expects a competent person overseeing fall protection on the site. Plan the fall-protection method **before** the crew leaves the ground each morning, not after someone is already 12 feet up.

title: Roof Rafter and Truss Basics: Layout, Bracing, and Tie-Downs
content:
## Roof Rafter and Truss Basics

### Stick-Framed Rafters

Rafters are sized from **IRC Table R802.4.1** based on species, snow/dead load, and spacing.
- `2x8 DF #2 @ 16" OC` rafters span roughly **13'-16'** depending on load.
- Cut a **plumb cut** at the ridge, a **bird's-mouth (seat cut)** at the wall plate (depth ≤ 1/4 the rafter depth per **IRC R802.7.1**), and a **tail/plumb cut** at the eave.
- A structural **ridge beam** is required when rafters can't form a triangle (cathedral, no ceiling ties); a non-structural ridge board is allowed when **ceiling joists/rafter ties** resist outward thrust per **IRC R802.4.5**.

### Roof Trusses

Engineered trusses arrive with a stamped layout and **truss design drawings (TDDs)**. The contractor must follow the **BCSI (Building Component Safety Information)** bracing guide.
- Set trusses at **24" OC** (typical), spread by the layout, and align with stacked wall studs.
- Install **temporary bracing** as you go — diagonal and lateral — to prevent the dominoes-style collapse that injures crews.
- **Permanent bracing**: top chord braced by sheathing, bottom chord and webs braced per the TDD.

### Tie-Downs and Uplift

Wind uplift must be resisted at each truss/rafter-to-plate connection:
- **Simpson Strong-Tie H2.5A**, **H1**, or **H10** hurricane ties — installed with the full nail count (typically **5) 8d x 1-1/2"** plus plate nails).
- High-wind zones use heavier **META/MGT** straps and a continuous load path down to the foundation hold-downs.

### Sheathing

- `7/16"` or `1/2"` OSB/plywood, strength axis across rafters, **8d at 6" edge / 12" field** per **IRC R803**.
- Use **plyclips (H-clips)** at unsupported panel edges between rafters at 24" OC.
- Leave a **1/8"** gap at panel edges.

### Ceiling Ties and Collar Ties

- **Rafter (ceiling) ties** near the top-plate level resist the outward thrust that would otherwise push walls apart — required for non-structural-ridge assemblies per **IRC R802.4.5**.
- **Collar ties** in the upper third resist ridge separation under wind uplift; install per **IRC R802.4.6**, typically `1x4` min at 4'-0" OC.
- Where a structural ridge beam is used, rafters bear on the beam and ties may not be required — but the ridge beam and its posts must be sized and supported to the foundation.

### Verification

- Confirm **heel height, overhang, pitch, and bearing** match the plans and truss layout before sheathing.
- Verify every truss/rafter has its **uplift connector** fully nailed before the roof is loaded.
- **Never cut, notch, or modify a truss** (top chord, bottom chord, or web) without **written truss-engineer approval** and a repair detail — field alterations void the engineered design and create life-safety hazards.

Get the bracing, ties, and tie-downs right; the roof is the structure's hat against gravity and wind alike, and the most-watched assembly in a wind event.

title: Hanging Drywall: Screw Spacing, Ceilings First, and Type X Fire-Rated Board
content:
## Hanging Drywall Correctly

### Board Selection

- **USG Sheetrock 1/2"** regular for most walls and ceilings at **16" OC**.
- **1/2" sag-resistant (USG Sheetrock UltraLight Ceiling)** for ceilings at **24" OC** — standard 1/2" sags at 24" OC.
- **5/8" Type X** fire-rated for garages, ceilings, party walls, and any rated assembly (**IRC R302**). **National Gypsum Gold Bond Fire-Shield** and **CertainTeed Type X** are equivalents.
- Run sheets **perpendicular** to framing to bridge more members and stagger butt joints.

### Hang the Ceiling First

Always hang **ceilings before walls** so wall sheets support the ceiling edges. Use a **drywall lift** or a deadman `T-brace` and a helper. Push tight to framing — gaps cause screw pops and cracks.

### Screw Spacing — IRC R702.3.5

- **Ceilings:** screws at **12" OC** in the field (7" OC if nails).
- **Walls:** screws at **16" OC** in the field.
- Keep fasteners **3/8" from edges**.
- Use **#6 coarse-thread drywall screws** for wood framing (`1-1/4"` for 1/2", `1-5/8"` for 5/8"). **Fine-thread #6** for steel studs.
- Set screws to **dimple** the paper **without breaking it** — a **DeWalt** or **Makita** drywall screw gun with an adjustable nose-cone sets perfect depth every time. A torn face paper has near-zero holding power.

### Cutting and Fitting

- Score the face paper with a utility knife, snap, cut the back paper.
- Use a **rotary cut-out tool (RotoZip / DeWalt)** for outlets — measure twice; over-cut boxes are a finishing headache.
- Maintain a **1/4" gap** at the floor (kept off the floor with a foot lifter) so the board doesn't wick moisture and so panels seat tight to the ceiling.

### Fastening Strategy

- Fasten from the **center of the sheet outward** to avoid bowing.
- Don't fasten within 1" of an untaped edge that meets another sheet — let the joint compound and tape do their work, but support both edges on framing.
- **Glue + screw** (construction adhesive bead on studs) reduces screw count and pops on walls.

### Field Tip

Butt joints are the hardest to finish flat. Place them on a **back-blocked** location or center them on a stud and feather wide. Minimize butt joints by buying the longest boards that fit (`12'`).

title: Taping and Finishing: Levels 0-5 and the Three-Coat System
content:
## Taping and Finishing to Levels 0-5

The **GA-214** finish levels define how smooth a wall must be for its final finish. Spec'ing and hitting the right level avoids callbacks and overwork.

### The Finish Levels

- **Level 0:** No taping/finishing — temporary or unfinished.
- **Level 1:** Tape embedded in joint compound; fire/smoke barriers above ceilings, plenums.
- **Level 2:** Tape + one coat over fasteners; garages, behind tile.
- **Level 3:** Two coats over joints/fasteners; medium/heavy textures.
- **Level 4:** Three coats; flat paints, light textures, most residential walls.
- **Level 5:** Level 4 + a **skim coat** of joint compound or high-build primer over the entire surface; required for **gloss/semi-gloss paint** and **critical raking light** (large windows). Use **USG Sheetrock Tuff-Hide** or a thinned **Plus 3** skim.

### The Three-Coat System

1. **Embed coat (tape coat):** Apply **USG All-Purpose** joint compound into the joint, embed **paper tape** (or self-adhesive **FibaTape mesh** on flat joints with setting-type compound). Wipe to bed the tape with a `5"-6"` knife; squeeze out excess. Mesh tape must be used with **setting-type (hot mud)** like **USG Durabond/Easy Sand** to prevent cracking.
2. **Fill coat:** After dry (24 hrs for All-Purpose, faster for setting types), apply a wider `8"-10"` coat, feathering edges. Coat screws again.
3. **Finish/skim coat:** A `10"-12"` final feather with **USG Plus 3** (lightweight, sands easily, low shrinkage). Feather butt joints out **16"-24"** each side.

### Sanding and Inspection

- Sand between coats only as needed with **150-220 grit** on a pole sander; final sand with **220**.
- Use a **drywall sander with HEPA vacuum (Festool Planex / DeWalt)** to control dust.
- **Light test:** Sweep a halogen/LED work light across the wall at a low angle to catch ridges and pinholes before primer.

### Compound Types and When to Use Them

- **All-purpose (USG All-Purpose / green lid):** good adhesion and crack resistance for embedding tape; dries slow (~24 hrs), shrinks more.
- **Topping / lightweight (USG Plus 3 / blue lid):** low shrinkage, sands easily — ideal for second and finish coats. Don't embed tape with topping; it bonds weaker.
- **Setting-type (USG Easy Sand / Durabond 20-45-90-210):** chemically hardens in the named minutes regardless of humidity. Use for first coats, mesh tape, deep fills, and same-day recoats; **Durabond** is very hard to sand (use Easy Sand for sandable setting mud).

### Pro Notes

- **Setting-type compound** (Easy Sand 20/45/90) for first coats speeds same-day recoating and resists shrinkage; **lightweight all-purpose (Plus 3)** for final coats sands easily.
- Don't over-sand into the tape — **three thin, wide coats** beat one thick coat every time.
- Box and tube tools (**auto-taper, flat boxes, angle heads**) dramatically speed production work and lay a more consistent crown than hand-finishing.
- Always **prime with a dedicated drywall primer-sealer** before topcoat to equalize the suction difference between paper and compound.

title: Corner Bead and Inside/Outside Corners Done Right
content:
## Corners: Inside and Outside

Corners are where drywall jobs are judged. Straight, chip-resistant corners read as quality.

### Outside Corners

Protect outside corners with **corner bead**:
- **Metal (galvanized) bead** — nailed/screwed/crimped every **8-9"**. Classic and durable but dents.
- **Paper-faced metal bead (USG Sheetrock Beadex)** — bedded in joint compound with a corner roller/applicator; superior bond, fewer pops.
- **Vinyl bead** — won't rust; good for high-moisture areas.
- **No-Coat (Trim-Tex/No-Coat) flexible bead** — for **off-angle and arched** corners and bullnose; sets ultra-straight and resists cracking. **Trim-Tex** vinyl beads are a pro favorite.

**Installation:**
1. Set the bead plumb and straight — a bowed bead telegraphs through every coat.
2. For paper-faced: trowel **USG All-Purpose** on both walls, press bead in, wipe both flanges. For metal: fasten then coat.
3. Three coats, feathering **6", 9", 12"** off the nose. Run a knife along the bead nose as a screed.

### Inside Corners

- Fold **paper tape** along its center crease; embed in compound on both walls with a `5"` knife or a **corner trowel / inside corner roller**.
- Wipe each side to bed, leaving no trapped air or wrinkles. Trapped air = bubbles that telegraph and crack.
- Apply a fill and finish coat to **one side at a time** (let dry between) so your knife rides clean against the adjacent dry side.

### Bullnose and Specialty

- **Bullnose corners** use specialty bead (**Trim-Tex Bullnose**) with matching transition/adapter pieces at intersections.
